{{Short description|Predicate which can take declarative or interrogative subclause}}
In [[formal semantics (natural language)|formal semantics]] a '''responsive predicate''' is an embedding predicate which can take either a [[Declarative sentence|declarative]] or an [[interrogative]] [[embedded clause|complement]]. For instance, the [[English language|English]] [[verb]] ''know'' is responsive as shown by the following examples.<ref>{{cite book |last= Lahiri |first= Utpal |year = 2002 |title= Questions and answers in embedded contexts | publisher= Oxford University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Theiler |first1= Nadine |last2= Roelofsen |first2= Floris | last3=Aloni | first3=Maria|author3-link=Maria Aloni |year= 2019 |title= Picky predicates: Why believe doesn't like interrogative complements, and other puzzles |journal= Natural Language Semantics |volume= 27 |issue= 2|pages= 95–134 |doi= 10.1007/s11050-019-09152-9 |s2cid= 254873164 |doi-access= free |hdl= 11245.1/614b1fa0-70cf-4edb-bd1e-eb13a6838857 |hdl-access= free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Elliott |first1=Patrick |last2=Klinedinst |first2=Nathan | last3=Sudo |first3=Yasutada | last4=Uegaki |first4=Wataru |year=2017 |title= Predicates of relevance and theories of question embedding |url= |journal= Journal of Semantics |volume=34 |issue=3 }}</ref>

# Bill knows whether Mary left.
# Bill knows that Mary left.

Responsives are contrasted with ''rogatives'' such as ''wonder'' which can only take an interrogative complement and ''anti-rogatives'' such as ''believe'' which can only take a declarative complement.

# Bill wonders whether Mary left.
# *Bill wonders that Mary left.
# *Bill believes whether Mary left.
#  Bill believes that Mary left.

Some analyses have derived these distinctions from [[type theory|type compatibility]] while others explain them in terms of particular properties of the embedding verbs and their complements.
